points: Volitional Form + と思っています

title: Let's (casual) and plans
canDo: I can make the volitional form of any verb: 見る → 見よう, 飲む → 飲もう, 帰る → 帰ろう, する → しよう, 来る → 来よう.
I can invite a friend in casual speech (いっしょに行こう！, 行こうよ) and ask what we should do together (何を食べようか。).
I can offer to help in casual speech: 持とうか。, 手伝おうか。
I can talk about plans I have been thinking about with 〜ようと思っています, both my own and other people's.
I can tell apart 行こうと思っています (a plan), 行くと思います (an opinion) and 行くつもりです (a firmer intention).

blocks.t: Warm-up: say the dictionary form and the 〜ましょう form of 8 verbs out loud (lessons 05-3 and 08-1), naming the type of each one (る-verb, う-verb or irregular)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 3 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬
Lesson 15 video (block 6), only the part on the volitional form
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: The dictionary form of every verb, knowing whether each one is a る-verb, an う-verb or irregular (lessons 03-1 and 08-1). The volitional comes straight from it.
〜ましょう and 〜ましょうか (lessons 05-3 and 06-4): the volitional is the casual version of both.
Casual speech (lesson 08-1): who you can use it with, and who you can't.
〜と思います (lesson 08-2) and 〜つもりです (lesson 10-2), which come back in point c.
〜そうです for appearance (lesson 13-2), which shows up in one example (重そう).

vocab.en: trip, travel (旅行する = to travel)
to move (to a new home) (volitional: ひっこそう)
to quit, to stop doing (タバコをやめる) (volitional: やめよう)
to go back, to return (home). An う-verb: 帰ろう
to enter, to go into (おんせんに入る). An う-verb: 入ろう
to hold, to carry (volitional: 持とう)
to rest, to take a break (volitional: 休もう)
to look up, to check, to research
Hokkaido (the big island in the north of Japan)
to be a help (たすかる！ = "that really helps!")
I'm thinking of…, I plan to… (after the volitional)

grammar.title: Forming it: 見よう, 飲もう, しよう, 来よう
grammar.explanation:
The **volitional form** is the casual version of 〜ましょう (lesson 05-3): it is the "let's…!" you say to friends and family. The name comes from "volition", your will: it also expresses **your will to do something**, and that is why it will help you talk about plans in point c. Like almost every new form, it comes from the **dictionary form** (lesson 08-1), and the verb type decides the path.
• **る-verbs**: drop る and add **よう**. 食べ|る → 食べ|よう; 見る → 見よう; 起きる → 起きよう.
• **う-verbs**: change the final **u** to the **o** of the same kana row and add **う**. 行く (ik**u**) → 行こう (ik**ō**); 飲む → 飲もう; 話す → 話そう; 待つ → 待とう; 帰る → 帰ろう; およぐ → およごう; あそぶ → あそぼう. Verbs ending in う go to お: 買う → 買おう; 手伝う → 手伝おう.
• **Irregular verbs**: **する → しよう** (勉強する → 勉強しよう) and **来る → 来よう**, read こよう, with こ.
• **The final う is a long sound.** 行こう is read i-ko-o, three equal beats, and romaji marks it with a macron: ikō. It is the same long vowel as in ありがとう.
• Quick clue: the volitional of an う-verb always ends in **-ō** (-kō, -mō, -rō…); the volitional of a る-verb always ends in **-yō**.
• In the sentence, the volitional is the **PREDICATE**, at the end, in the same slot as ましょう. Nothing else changes: [when] [with whom] [where] [what] + volitional.
grammar.structure: る-verbs: [stem] + よう · う-verbs: u → o + う · する → しよう · 来る → 来よう (こよう)

examples.jp: 週末、いっしょに映画を見よう。
examples.kana: しゅうまつ、いっしょにえいがをみよう。
examples.romaji: Shūmatsu, issho ni eiga o miyō.
examples.en: Let's watch a movie together this weekend.

examples.jp: もう九時だ。そろそろ帰ろう。
examples.kana: もうくじだ。そろそろかえろう。
examples.en: It's already nine. Let's head home soon. [lit. soon, let's go home]

examples.jp: この店、おいしかったね。また来ようね。
examples.kana: このみせ、おいしかったね。またこようね。
examples.romaji: Kono mise, oishikatta ne. Mata koyō ne.
examples.en: This restaurant was delicious, wasn't it? Let's come again, OK?

pitfalls: Don't add よう after a whole う-verb: 飲むよう ✗ → 飲もう ✓. よう belongs only to る-verbs; with う-verbs, the last syllable itself changes.
帰る and 入る end in る, but they are う-verbs: 帰よう ✗ → 帰ろう ✓ (かえ|る → かえ|ろう); 入よう ✗ → 入ろう ✓.
来る becomes こよう, with こ: きよう ✗, くよう ✗ → 来よう (こよう) ✓. And する becomes しよう: するよう ✗ → しよう ✓.
In writing, keep the long う: 行こ ✗ in your homework → 行こう ✓. In messages between friends you will see 行こ！ or 帰ろ！, without the う. That is very informal: recognize it, but don't copy it.
howToStudy: Make a table in your notebook with 12 verbs (4 る-verbs, 6 う-verbs, する and 来る) in three columns: dictionary form → 〜ましょう → volitional. Read it aloud, line by line: 飲む → 飲みましょう → 飲もう. Mark 帰る and 入る in color.

Tap 🔬 on example 2. The first sentence has its own ★ PREDICATE (九時だ); in the second, そろそろ shows up as HOW / HOW OFTEN and 帰ろう as ★ PREDICATE, of the invitation / suggestion kind — the same kind as 〜ましょう. The volitional simply took the place of ましょう.
Say 6 invitations to a friend out loud, each with a different type of verb: 映画を見よう、コーヒーを飲もう、ゲームをしよう、公園であそぼう…
grammar.flag: Check in your Genki II that this lesson has these points in this order.

grammar.title: Uses: inviting, asking and offering (〜よう / 〜ようか)
grammar.gloss: the everyday 〜ましょう / 〜ましょうか
grammar.explanation:
In casual speech, the volitional does everything 〜ましょう and 〜ましょうか do in polite speech. Always compare it with the polite form you already know:
• **Inviting, already expecting a "yes"**: 行きましょう → **行こう！** ("let's go!"). With **よ** at the end, the invitation gets a little push: 行こうよ ("come on, let's go!").
• **Asking what to do together**: 何を食べましょうか → **何を食べようか**. Without a question word, it means "shall we…?": ちょっと休もうか ("shall we take a short break?"). In speech you will also hear 食べよっか.
• **Offering to help** (lesson 06-4): 持ちましょうか → **持とうか** ("want me to carry it?"). The context shows who will do it: here, only you.
• **Talking to yourself**: on its own, the volitional is a decision said out loud. よし、がんばろう！ ("OK, I'm going to do my best!"); どうしよう！ ("what am I going to do?!").
• **Who to use it with**: friends, family and close colleagues, like every short form (lesson 08-1). With a teacher, a boss or someone you have just met, stay with 〜ましょう / 〜ましょうか, or invite with 〜ませんか (lesson 03-3).
• In the sentence, the volitional is the ★ PREDICATE. In a question with the volitional, か stays (食べようか). It is the same か as in 〜ましょうか, and here it does not sound blunt.
grammar.structure: […] volitional！ (let's) · volitional + よ (come on, let's!) · [question word] … volitional + か · volitional + か (want me to…?)

examples.jp: ばんごはん、何を食べようか。— ラーメンを食べに行こう。
examples.kana: ばんごはん、なにをたべようか。— ラーメンをたべにいこう。
examples.romaji: Bangohan, nani o tabeyō ka. — Rāmen o tabe ni ikō.
examples.en: What shall we have for dinner? — Let's go eat ramen.

examples.jp: にもつ、重そうだね。持とうか。— ありがとう、たすかる。
examples.kana: にもつ、おもそうだね。もとうか。— ありがとう、たすかる。
examples.romaji: Nimotsu, omosō da ne. Motō ka. — Arigatō, tasukaru.
examples.en: Your bags look heavy. Want me to carry them? — Thanks, that really helps.

examples.jp: ねえ、カラオケに行こうよ。— ごめん、今日はちょっと…。
examples.kana: ねえ、カラオケにいこうよ。— ごめん、きょうはちょっと…。
examples.romaji: Nē, karaoke ni ikō yo. — Gomen, kyō wa chotto….
examples.en: Hey, come on, let's go to karaoke! — Sorry, today is a bit…

pitfalls: The volitional is casual. With your teacher: 先生、いっしょに写真をとろう ✗ → 先生、いっしょに写真をとりましょう ✓ (or とりませんか).

The volitional includes you: it means "let's" or "I'll", never an order. 早くねよう = "let's go to bed early" (or "I'll go to bed early"). To ask a friend to do something, use the て-form, the casual version of 〜てください: 早くねて ✓.
〜ようよ pushes a little. With someone who may not be able to come, ask first: カラオケ、行かない？ (the casual version of 〜ませんか), and save 行こう for after the yes.
何を食べようか asks what we will do together, not what the other person wants. To ask what they want, use 〜たい (lesson 11-1): 何が食べたい？ ✓.
howToStudy: Say each example out loud in polite speech: 何を食べましょうか → ラーメンを食べに行きましょう; 持ちましょうか; カラオケに行きましょう. Then go back to the casual version and notice that only the ending changes.

Tap 🔬 on example 1. ばんごはん shows up as TIME ("for dinner"), 何を as OBJECT and 食べようか as ★ PREDICATE, of the invitation / suggestion kind. In the answer, 食べに shows up as PURPOSE and 行こう is the PREDICATE: let's go → to do what? → eat ramen.
Imagine a Saturday with a friend and write 4 lines in your notebook: 1 invitation (〜よう！), 1 with よ, 1 question with 何を or どこに + 〜ようか, and 1 offer to help (〜ようか).

grammar.title: Plans: 〜ようと思っています (vs. つもり)
grammar.gloss: I'm thinking of…, I plan to…
grammar.explanation:
To talk about a plan, attach **と思っています** to the volitional: 行こう + と思っています = "I'm thinking of going", "I plan to go". The logic is the one from lesson 08-2: と marks **what is thought**, and here the thought is "I'll do X".
• **〜ようと思っています**: a plan you **have been thinking about** for a while. The ている shows that the idea is still in your head. It is the most common way to talk about plans: 来年、日本で働こうと思っています。
• **〜ようと思います**, without ている: it sounds like a decision made **right now**, as you speak, like "I think I'll…": じゃあ、今日は早くねようと思います。
• **Someone else's plan**: always use **〜ようと思っています**: マリアさんは、来月ひっこそうと思っています。 With 思います, the sentence can only talk about what you yourself think.
• **The sentence stays polite.** The volitional sits inside the quote, and the ending decides the register: 思っています is polite; 思ってる is casual (ている → てる).

**Three sentences that look alike:**
• 行こうと思っています = "I'm thinking of going" (**my plan**).
• 行くと思います = "I think [he] will go" (**an opinion**, lesson 08-2). The only difference is the verb form: volitional vs. dictionary form.
• 行くつもりです = "I intend to go" (**an intention**, lesson 10-2). つもり comes after the dictionary form and usually sounds firmer, like a decision already made. 〜ようと思っています sounds more like "I'm thinking of", a plan that can still change. In practice, both work for talking about plans.
• For **negative** plans ("I plan not to…"), use 〜ないつもりです: 今日は飲まないつもりです. The volitional has almost no negative in everyday speech.
• In the sentence, 思っています is the ★ PREDICATE, and the volitional + と block is the **QUOTE**: the content of the plan. What comes before it (when, where, with whom) is part of the plan.
grammar.structure: [volitional] と思っています (a plan I've been thinking about) · [volitional] と思います (a decision made now) · vs. [dictionary form] つもりです

examples.jp: 来年、日本で働こうと思っています。
examples.kana: らいねん、にほんではたらこうとおもっています。
examples.romaji: Rainen, Nihon de hatarakō to omotte imasu.
examples.en: I'm thinking of working in Japan next year.

examples.jp: マリアさんは、来月ひっこそうと思っています。
examples.kana: マリアさんは、らいげつひっこそうとおもっています。
examples.romaji: Maria-san wa, raigetsu hikkosō to omotte imasu.
examples.en: Maria is thinking of moving next month.

examples.jp: 夏休みはどうするの？— まだきめていないけど、北海道に行こうと思ってる。
examples.kana: なつやすみはどうするの？— まだきめていないけど、ほっかいどうにいこうとおもってる。
examples.romaji: Natsuyasumi wa dō suru no? — Mada kimete inai kedo, Hokkaidō ni ikō to omotteru.
examples.en: What are you doing for summer vacation? — I haven't decided yet, but I'm thinking of going to Hokkaido.

pitfalls: For your own plan, use the volitional: 行くと思っています sounds like "I think (someone) will go" ✗ → 行こうと思っています ✓.
No ましょう inside the quote: 行きましょうと思っています ✗ → 行こうと思っています ✓. The politeness goes only at the end (思っています).
Someone else's plan needs ている: マリアさんはひっこそうと思います ✗ → マリアさんはひっこそうと思っています ✓.
Don't mix the two patterns: 行こうつもりです ✗. Use 行くつもりです ✓ or 行こうと思っています ✓.
howToStudy: Tap 🔬 on example 1. 来年 shows up as TIME, 日本で as PLACE, 働こうと as QUOTE and 思っています as ★ PREDICATE (ongoing / state). Read it from the end: I'm thinking → of what? working → where? in Japan → when? next year.
Say 3 pairs out loud and say in English what each sentence means: 行こうと思っています vs. 行くと思います; 買おうと思っています vs. 買うと思います; 来ようと思っています vs. 来ると思います.
Write 3 true plans of yours in your notebook with 〜ようと思っています, and rewrite one of them with 〜つもりです. Read both out loud: which one sounds more decided?

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write with the kanji you already know and the rest in kana. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day. If you have the Genki II Workbook, do this lesson's exercises too — in this lesson, the ones on the volitional form and on 〜ようと思っています.

tasks.prompt: Change each verb to the volitional form. Before writing, decide the verb type: る-verb, う-verb or irregular.

items.note: A る-verb: drop る and add よう.
An う-verb: む (mu) → も (mo) + う.
帰る looks like a る-verb, but it is an う-verb: かえ|る → かえ|ろう.
Irregular, with こ: こよう.

tasks.prompt: Change from polite to casual speech by replacing 〜ましょう(か) with the volitional.

items.q: いっしょに帰りましょう。

items.note: With the volitional, the question's か stays.

items.q: ここで写真をとりましょう。

a.kana: ここでしゃしんをとろう。

items.note: This one is an offer: "want me to help?"

items.q: ちょっと休みましょう。
あしたは早く来ましょう。

a.kana: あしたははやくこよう。

tasks.prompt: Translate into Japanese. Careful: not every "I think" or "I'm thinking of" becomes the volitional.

items.q: I'm thinking of studying abroad in Japan next year.

a.jp: 来年、日本に留学しようと思っています。
a.kana: らいねん、にほんにりゅうがくしようとおもっています。
a.romaji: Rainen, Nihon ni ryūgaku shiyō to omotte imasu.

items.note: 留学する → 留学しよう. A plan you have been thinking about: と思っています.

items.q: I think Maria will come tomorrow.

a.jp: マリアさんはあした来ると思います。
a.kana: マリアさんはあしたくるとおもいます。
a.romaji: Maria-san wa ashita kuru to omoimasu.

items.note: This is an opinion about someone else, not a plan: dictionary form (来る).

items.q: Lucas is thinking of buying a new car.

a.jp: ルーカスさんは新しい車を買おうと思っています。
a.kana: ルーカスさんはあたらしいくるまをかおうとおもっています。
a.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa atarashii kuruma o kaō to omotte imasu.

items.note: Someone else's plan: always 〜と思っています.

items.q: (deciding right now) Well then, I think I'll go to bed early today.

a.jp: じゃあ、今日は早くねようと思います。
a.kana: じゃあ、きょうははやくねようとおもいます。
a.romaji: Jā, kyō wa hayaku neyō to omoimasu.

items.note: A decision made in the moment: 〜ようと思います, without ている.

items.q: I plan not to drink (alcohol) today. (use つもり)

a.jp: 今日はおさけを飲まないつもりです。
a.kana: きょうはおさけをのまないつもりです。
a.romaji: Kyō wa osake o nomanai tsumori desu.

items.note: A negative plan: 〜ないつもりです. The volitional has almost no negative in everyday speech.

items.q: (casual, to a friend) It's raining, huh. Shall we take a taxi?

a.jp: 雨がふっているね。タクシーに乗ろうか。
a.kana: あめがふっているね。タクシーにのろうか。
a.romaji: Ame ga futte iru ne. Takushī ni norō ka.

items.note: 乗る is an う-verb: 乗ろう. タクシーに: the に of getting into a vehicle.

tasks.prompt: A Japanese friend asked you: 今度の休みは何をするの？ Answer in casual speech, in 5 sentences: 2 plans with 〜ようと思ってる, 1 negative plan with 〜ないつもり, 1 invitation for your friend to come along (〜ようよ) and 1 offer (〜ようか). Then read it aloud and record it on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: 北海道に行こうと思ってる。おんせんにも入ろうと思ってる。でも、スキーはしないつもり。いっしょに行こうよ！ホテル、しらべようか。
a.kana: ほっかいどうにいこうとおもってる。おんせんにもはいろうとおもってる。でも、スキーはしないつもり。いっしょにいこうよ！ホテル、しらべようか。
a.romaji: Hokkaidō ni ikō to omotteru. Onsen ni mo hairō to omotteru. Demo, sukī wa shinai tsumori. Issho ni ikō yo! Hoteru, shirabeyō ka.
a.en: I'm thinking of going to Hokkaido. I'm thinking of going into a hot spring, too. But I'm not planning to ski. Come on, let's go together! Want me to look up hotels?

items.note: Check: the volitional + と思ってる for the plans (not the dictionary form), 〜ないつもり for the negative, よ in the invitation and か in the offer. Since it's for a friend, no です／ます.

practice.what: Play normally, preferably in an N4-level area if you have reached one. Hunt the dialogues for volitionals: endings in 〜おう / 〜よう (行こう, 見よう, しよう) and plans with 〜ようと思って. When you find one, say out loud the matching polite form (行きましょう) or, if it's a plan, what the character intends to do. Log the session in Immersion → Games and paste one of those lines into 🔬 Anatomy.
Drills → Conjugation: warm up with the dictionary form, the base of the volitional. Then Drills → 🔬 Anatomy → 🧱 Build from the end with example 1 of point c, starting from 思っています.
In the ヅオリンゴー Journal, write 3 true plans with 〜ようと思っています and 1 with 〜つもりです. Open "Anatomy of what I wrote" and check that the volitional + と block shows up as QUOTE.
Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. Hold the long sound at the end: か・え・ろ・う is 4 beats, and ろう must not shrink to ろ.
Record your answer to homework h4 in 30 seconds or less, like a voice message to your friend. Listen and check that the plans came out with the volitional (〜おう / 〜よう), not the dictionary form.

culture.title: School trips (しゅうがくりょこう)
culture.body: In Japan, the whole class usually goes on a **しゅうがくりょこう** (修学旅行): a study trip of a few days, generally in the last or second-to-last year of each stage of school. Classic destinations tend to be historic cities like Kyoto and Nara, and also Hiroshima and Okinawa, where students learn about the history of war and peace; some high schools even travel abroad. The itinerary is planned well in advance, and at many schools the students split into small groups called **はん**, which make their own plan for the free time. At night, the class usually sleeps at a ryokan (a traditional inn), several students to a room, on futons laid out on the floor. For many Japanese people, this trip is one of the most vivid memories of their school years.
culture.try: Imagine you are in a はん in Kyoto, planning your free afternoon. Write 3 casual lines with the volitional (おてらに行こう！, お昼は何を食べようか。…) and 1 polite sentence telling the teacher what the group plans to do, with 〜ようと思っています.

checklist: I can make the volitional of any verb without looking: る → よう, う → o + う, する → しよう, 来る → 来よう.
I remember that 帰る and 入る are う-verbs: 帰ろう, 入ろう.
I can invite a friend with 〜よう(よ), ask with 〜ようか and offer to help (持とうか).
I know the volitional is casual, and I switch to 〜ましょう with a teacher or a boss.
I can talk about plans with 〜ようと思っています, both mine and other people's.
I can tell apart 行こうと思っています (a plan), 行くと思います (an opinion) and 行くつもりです (an intention).
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
If I have the Genki II Workbook: I did the exercises on the volitional form and on 〜ようと思っています.
